title: Workflows as agents, sub-workflows and declarative workflows
summary: Three ways to compose and reuse workflows: expose one as an agent, nest one inside another as an executor, or define the graph in YAML instead of code.
useIf: A graph must plug into agent-shaped hosts (A2A, Responses, AG-UI), a workflow is reusable inside larger ones, or non-developers should edit the flow.
avoidIf: You expect middleware on the wrapper to protect inner agents, or you need complex custom logic that YAML actions cannot express.

explain.md: **Workflow as agent.** Python `workflow.as_agent(name=...)`, .NET `workflow.AsAIAgent(id, name, description)`. The start executor must accept chat messages (agent-based executors do). It gets sessions: a serialized session contains the inner workflow checkpoint. Requests raised inside surface to the caller as function calls (Python name `WorkflowAgent.REQUEST_INFO_FUNCTION_NAME`), and you answer with a function result. Python 1.2.2 (2026-04-29) made orchestration output an `AgentResponse`, so `as_agent()` returns only the final answer [[tr20]] [[tr49]].

explain.title: The wrapper does not carry policy
explain.md: In Python, middleware configured on the wrapper agent does not run, and instructions, tools and chat or function middleware contributed by wrapper context providers do not flow into workflow executors. Configure required policy on the agents or clients inside the workflow. In .NET the `id` passed to `AsAIAgent` names only the outer agent: inner agents still need stable `ChatClientAgentOptions.Id` values for checkpoint resume [[tr20]].

**Sub-workflows.** Python wraps a workflow in `WorkflowExecutor(workflow=inner, id=..., allow_direct_output=False, propagate_request=False)`; .NET uses `BindAsExecutor`. The inner workflow runs as one step of the parent with its own superstep loop and independent state, and the parent checkpoint carries inner state. With `propagate_request=False` requests from the inner graph arrive at parent executors as `SubWorkflowRequestMessage` (answer with `request.create_response(...)` and `target_id=request.executor_id`); with `True` they surface as ordinary request events to the caller. Nesting can be multi-level [[tr21]].

**Declarative.** YAML defines actions instead of code. Python shape: `name`, `description`, `inputs`, `actions`; C#: `kind: Workflow` with `trigger.kind: OnConversationStart`, `trigger.id`, `trigger.actions`. Action families cover variables, control flow, agent and tool calls (`InvokeAzureAgent`, `InvokeFunctionTool`), HTTP and MCP, human input (`Question`, `RequestExternalInput`) and conversation control. The docs advise declarative for standard patterns and frequently changing flows, code for complex custom logic [[tr22]]. Python 1.7.0 (2026-05-28) removed Python-only actions and renamed alias kinds to the C# canonical names.

blocks.code:
inner = (WorkflowBuilder(start_executor=specialist1)
         .add_edge(specialist1, specialist2).build())
analysis = WorkflowExecutor(workflow=inner, id='analysis-pipeline',
                            propagate_request=True)
parent = (WorkflowBuilder(start_executor=coordinator)
          .add_edge(coordinator, analysis)
          .add_edge(analysis, reviewer).build())

pipeline_agent = parent.as_agent(name='Content Pipeline Agent')
response = await pipeline_agent.run('Write about AI trends')

name: greeting-workflow
description: Greets the user
inputs:
  name:
    type: string
actions:
  - kind: SetVariable
    id: build_message
    variable: Local.message
    value: =Concat("Hello, ", Workflow.Inputs.name, "!")
  - kind: InvokeAzureAgent
    id: call_assistant
    agent:
      name: AssistantAgent
    input:
      messages: =Local.message
    output:
      autoSend: true

whereToUse: Exposing an orchestration over A2A, AG-UI or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which speak the agent interface
Reusing a verified review pipeline as one step in several parent workflows
Letting analysts or product owners edit routing and prompts in YAML without a deploy of code
Hosting a workflow in a Foundry hosted agent (prefer native workflow hosting over `as_agent`)

use: The consumer expects an agent (chat messages in, response out)
A graph is a reusable component with a clear input and output
The flow is a standard pattern that changes often
avoid: You need wrapper-level guardrails: put them inside the workflow's agents
Complex custom logic or integration with existing Python code: write the graph in code
Hosting a stateful `WorkflowAgent` for many users from one instance: it keeps workflow state in memory
flips: Requests inside the inner graph should reach a human directly: set `propagate_request=True`; to answer them in the parent, keep the default and add a handler
Foundry Responses hosting: host the workflow natively with `workflow=` and a request-aware factory instead of `agent=workflow.as_agent()` (deprecated)

pitfalls.symptom: A guardrail on the workflow agent never fires
pitfalls.cause: Middleware on the Python wrapper does not execute for inner agents
pitfalls.fix: Attach middleware to the agents or clients inside the workflow

pitfalls.symptom: Resume of a serialized workflow-agent session fails in .NET
pitfalls.cause: Inner agents were recreated with different ids; the outer `AsAIAgent` id does not stabilise them
pitfalls.fix: Set stable `ChatClientAgentOptions.Id` (and unchanged `Name`) for every inner agent

pitfalls.symptom: Old YAML stops loading after an upgrade
pitfalls.cause: Python 1.7.0 removed Python-only actions and renamed alias kinds; 1.0.0rc2 replaced `InvokeTool` with `InvokeFunctionTool`
pitfalls.fix: Rename kinds to the canonical names and test loading in CI

scenarios.title: Publish a review pipeline to other teams
scenarios.situation: A platform team has a workflow with draft, legal check and editor review. Five product teams want it as a tool for their own agents over A2A. Legal rules must always run.
unknowns: How many concurrent users per instance?
Is the workflow stateful across calls?
scenarios.question: How do you expose it?

options.name: Wrap with `as_agent()` or `AsAIAgent` for hosting, put legal guardrails on the inner agents, and use a per-request factory so no state is shared across users
options.why: The agent interface is what A2A and Responses hosts expect, inner policy always applies, and a factory avoids shared mutable state.
options.tradeoff: A fresh graph per request costs build time and needs stable ids for resume.

options.name: Wrap once and register one `WorkflowAgent` instance for all callers
options.why: A `WorkflowAgent` keeps workflow state in memory between runs, so one instance must never serve different users.

options.name: Put the legal check in wrapper middleware
options.why: Wrapper middleware does not run for inner agents in Python.
options.tradeoff: Right only for policies on the outer request that the inner graph does not need to see.

flips.if: You host on Foundry Responses in Python
flips.then: Host the workflow natively with `workflow=` and `parse_response`; `agent=workflow.as_agent()` is deprecated.

flips.if: Teams need to edit the legal text only
flips.then: Move prompts into YAML or files, not graph code.

scenarios.takeaway: Wrap for the host, enforce policy inside, and never share one stateful instance.

scenarios.title: Business owners tweak a routing flow
scenarios.situation: A support routing flow changes weekly: new queues, new questions, different agent prompts. Business analysts own the content. Developers own deployment.
unknowns: Do any steps need custom code?
scenarios.question: Code or YAML?

options.name: Declarative YAML for the flow, custom code only for steps YAML cannot express, with load tests in CI
options.why: The docs recommend declarative for standard patterns and frequently changing flows.
options.tradeoff: Action kinds changed during 2026, so pin versions and test loads on upgrade.

options.name: A programmatic graph in code
options.tradeoff: Every change is a developer deploy.

options.name: One big agent with a long prompt listing queues
options.why: Routing becomes non-deterministic and hard to audit.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for a small, low-risk router.

flips.if: Routing needs complex logic or calls into existing Python services

flips.then: Keep YAML in version control with review.

scenarios.takeaway: Declarative is for flows that change more often than the code around them.
